cards.headline: Sleep is when training sinks in
lines: Sleep-medicine groups recommend 8–10 hours a night for teens and at least 7 for adults.
Deep sleep is when growth hormone peaks and much of the body's repair happens.
In one study of young athletes, those sleeping under 8 hours were injured more often.
cards.source: Paruthi et al. (2016), AASM consensus, J Clin Sleep Med; Milewski et al. (2014), J Pediatr Orthop.

cards.headline: Fast and slow muscle fibres
lines: Slow-twitch (type I) fibres resist fatigue and power endurance.
Fast-twitch (type II) fibres produce force quickly but tire sooner.
Everyone has a mix, and training changes how each type performs.

cards.headline: Why warming up works
lines: Light movement raises muscle temperature, helping muscles contract faster and more forcefully.
Moving drills generally prepare you for sport better than long static holds.
Structured warm-ups such as FIFA 11+ have reduced injuries in youth football studies.
cards.source: Jeffreys (2007), the RAMP warm-up, Professional Strength & Conditioning; Soligard et al. (2008), BMJ.

cards.headline: Water and performance
lines: Losing around 2% of body weight in sweat can noticeably reduce endurance performance.
In long, hot sessions, the salts lost in sweat matter too.
Weighing before and after training shows how much fluid a session costs.

visual.caption: body-weight loss where endurance can dip

cards.source: Sawka et al. (2007), ACSM Position Stand: Exercise and Fluid Replacement.

cards.headline: Progressive overload
lines: Muscles, bones and tendons adapt to the demands placed on them.
Raise load, reps or difficulty gradually — then let the body recover.
Big, sudden jumps in training load are a well-known injury risk.
cards.source: ACSM (2009), progression models in resistance training; Gabbett (2016), British Journal of Sports Medicine.

cards.question: Why does your heart rate rise during exercise?
options: To get more oxygen to working muscles
cards.why: Working muscles need more oxygen and fuel, so the heart pumps more blood every minute.
cards.source: McArdle, Katch & Katch, 'Exercise Physiology', cardiovascular responses.

cards.question: Muscle soreness a day or two after hard exercise is mainly caused by…
options: Lactic acid left in the muscle
cards.why: Lactate clears within about an hour. Delayed soreness (DOMS) comes from tiny muscle damage and the repair that follows.
cards.source: Cheung, Hume & Maxwell (2003), 'Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness', Sports Medicine.

cards.question: What is the body's main fuel for high-intensity exercise?
cards.why: Muscles burn stored carbohydrate (glycogen) fastest. Fat fuels more of low-intensity work.

cards.question: How much sleep does the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommend for 13–18-year-olds?
cards.why: 8 to 10 hours a night, regularly, for teenagers.
cards.source: Paruthi et al. (2016), AASM consensus statement, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine.

cards.question: Right before sprinting, which warm-up is generally better?
options: Moving drills that build up speed
cards.why: Dynamic drills raise temperature and rehearse the movement; long static holds just before can slightly cut power.
cards.source: Behm & Chaouachi (2011), European Journal of Applied Physiology.

cards.headline: Your skeleton is always rebuilding
cards.text: Bone is broken down and laid down all the time. Over about ten years, most of an adult skeleton is replaced.
cards.source: Manolagas (2000), Endocrine Reviews; NIH, 'Bone Health and Osteoporosis' (2004).

cards.headline: A heart beats about 100,000 times a day
cards.text: At around 70 beats a minute, that's roughly 100,000 beats a day. Trained endurance athletes often have lower resting rates.

cards.headline: Elite endurance athletes have huge aerobic engines
cards.text: VO₂max — the most oxygen the body can use — can exceed 80 ml/kg/min in elite male endurance athletes, about double many untrained adults.
cards.source: McArdle, Katch & Katch, 'Exercise Physiology', maximal oxygen uptake.

cards.headline: Simple reaction time is about a fifth of a second
cards.text: Reacting to one expected signal takes around 0.2 s. Choosing between options takes longer, and more options take longer still (Hick's law).
cards.source: Hick (1952), Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology; Schmidt & Lee, 'Motor Control and Learning'.

cards.headline: The body's three energy systems

steps.headline: 1 · Phosphocreatine
lines: The fastest system powers all-out efforts of a few seconds: a sprint start, a jump.
It refills within a few minutes of rest.

steps.headline: 2 · Glycolytic
lines: For hard efforts of roughly 10 seconds to 2 minutes, carbohydrate is broken down fast without needing oxygen.
Powerful, but it can't last.

steps.headline: 3 · Aerobic
lines: For anything longer, the aerobic system uses oxygen to burn carbohydrate and fat.
Slower, but it can run for hours.

steps.headline: 4 · All at once
lines: The systems overlap — none is ever fully on or off.
A basketball game uses all three: sprints, repeated bursts, and the long game in between.

cards.source: Gastin (2001), 'Energy System Interaction', Sports Medicine; McArdle, Katch & Katch, 'Exercise Physiology'.

cards.headline: Health & sport science: the takeaways
points: Type I fibres endure; type II are fast.
Moving warm-ups prepare you to move.
Next-day soreness is repair, not lactic acid.
